title: Their Practice, Career, Life And Work
objective: Research the chosen real practitioner’s practice, career, life and work, using sources that support each fact.

blocks.text: BUILD · Art · Week 6. Trinity Arts Award Bronze. Their Practice, Career, Life And Work.
Objective: research four sides of your chosen artist and show where each fact came from.
Success evidence: your own account of practice, career, life and work, a source for each, and your reason for choosing this real artist.
My Creative Identity is about the choices you make in art. You can keep your private life private. This lesson uses public sources about real artists.
40 minutes. Use the checked source pack, your Part C file, paper and a pencil.

This deck evidences Bronze Part C, Arts inspiration: simple research into a real artist, craftsperson or practitioner’s practice, career, life and work, and why chosen. C1 establishes the choice and reason; C2 completes the four research areas. The source of award requirements is tools/artsaward/SPEC.json, Bronze only. ONE Attempted allowed overall. Any Not Attempted = Below Pass. The 10-file cap applies to the whole Bronze portfolio, not each part or lesson. Append today’s evidence to the existing Bronze-C file and record the actual file name plus page, slide or timecode. The three assessment areas are art form knowledge and understanding, creativity, and communication. Core, Extend and Challenge vary support within Bronze; all retain the same required evidence. Only an adviser trained at Bronze may assess; delivery is through a validated centre. Staff must confirm both, not assume either. Adults may scribe the pupil’s exact words but must not write a reason or research account for them. No practitioner meeting or booking is required for Bronze Part C. The strand is My Creative Identity: discuss artistic choices, not pupils’ private lives.

Before the lesson, prepare a named, checked source pack with at least two genuine choices. Suggested public primary sources: Barbara Hepworth Estate, Biography, https://barbarahepworth.org.uk/biography/ (1903, 1921–24 and 1925 entries); its Assembly of Sea Forms record, https://barbarahepworth.org.uk/sculptures/1972/assembly-of-sea-forms/; Henry Moore Foundation, Discover Henry Moore, https://henry-moore.org/discover-and-research/discover-henry-moore/, and Henry Moore’s story, https://henry-moore.org/discover-and-research/discover-henry-moore/henry-moores-story/. These are research sources, not places to visit. Staff check each selected passage, work caption and public URL before use. Give each artist a page with a clearly credited work image or accessible description, its title and medium, and short, faithful source extracts covering practice, career, life and work. Keep the original beside any plain-language gloss. Number the pack pages and identify the publisher, page title, URL and section on each. Select art-relevant public life facts, such as where an artist worked; omit distressing biographical detail. Have large print and a read-aloud version ready. No invented fallback artist or biography: if a source fails, use a second checked source. The model below is conditional on the checked Hepworth pages being in hand; otherwise model the same process with the actual pack and its exact facts. The deck does not certify a local pack as prepared.

stages.title: Arrival · retrieve
stages.data-ta1: Return each pupil’s C1 choice and locator. If it is missing, retrieve their existing evidence or let them make a fresh, sourced choice; do not assign a private-life comparison.

blocks.text: Find the artist and work you chose last time. Read your reason for that choice. What did you want to learn? Keep that question beside the checked source pack.
Today we build a picture with four parts. Practice means how the person makes art. Career means their path in art. Life means public facts about their life. Work means a piece they made.
A good account needs all four. Four notes on the same sculpture will not tell us about a career. A list of dates will not show how the artist works. We will use a different question for each part.
Your own life is not the subject of this task. Use art-relevant public facts about your chosen artist.

stages.title: Starter · create the need
stages.data-ta1: Show the deliberately thin anonymous note as a teaching example only, not a fictional practitioner for evidence. Ask pupils to match the questions to the headings.

blocks.text: Imagine a reader finds this note: A sculptor was born, went to art school and made a sculpture. The note has facts, but it gives very little to learn from.
Which sculptor? What did they learn? How did they make work? Which piece could we look at? A broad word can hide the thing we need to know.
Now set out four headings. Under each, write a question.

items: Practice: what tools, materials or ways of making did they use?
Career: how did they learn, work or develop as an artist?
Life: what checked public fact helps place their art in a time or place?
Work: what is a named piece, and what can I say about it?

blocks.text: These questions guide a search. They do not set a fixed number of facts for the award. A clear, checked note can do more than a page of copied text.

stages.title: I Do · model
stages.data-ta1: Use the named checked source entries while modelling. Show each heading on the original page. Facts are sourced teaching examples, not a pupil answer to copy or invented biographical placeholders.

blocks.text: I open the checked Hepworth pages. I read a small section, then choose the fact that answers my question. I do not copy the whole page.

For life, the 1903 entry places her birth in Wakefield. For career, the 1921–24 entry says she studied sculpture at the Royal College of Art. These facts do different jobs. One places a life; the other shows a step in training.

For practice, the 1925 entry tells us she learnt marble carving from Giovanni Ardini. I keep his name because it tells us who taught that skill. For work, the caption names Assembly of Sea Forms and white marble. I keep the title so the reader can find the piece.
I add the source beside each note. I use the page title and year heading for the life, career and practice notes. I use the work caption for the last note.

blocks.title: From a question to a checked note
blocks.caption: Keep the source beside the note it supports.
blocks.alt: Boxes labelled ASK, FIND, EXPLAIN, CHECK. Keep the source beside the note it supports.

blocks.text: Before I close the page, I read my note back against it. A shorter sentence must keep the same meaning. A source about one skill does not prove she used it in every work.

blocks.alt: A group of pale stone forms stands on a dark circular base. Rounded upright and low forms surround a taller central form with a small hole near its top.
blocks.caption: Barbara Hepworth, Assembly of Sea Forms, 1972, white marble (BH 555). Image and work details: Barbara Hepworth Estate. Collection: Norton Simon Museum, Pasadena.

blocks.text: Point to one shape or space that you want to learn more about. Check the caption for the material. Keep what you can see apart from what the source tells you.

blocks.label: Optional artist film: Henry Moore and forms from nature
blocks.text: If you choose Moore, watch a short passage selected by your teacher. Name one natural form and one making action. Keep a source note. Offline, use the picture and checked source notes in this pack.

Preview the optional Foundation film and its access support before class. Select a short passage within the existing model time, or use the included picture and source notes. The film is an alternative research source, not an extra required task.

stages.title: We Do · everyone commits
stages.data-ta1: Offer the on-screen controls, the matching paper task, speech or pointing. Model one response, then ask for a reason. Keep the practical work in the next stage.

data.heading: Four questions about one artist
data.instruction: Sort the checked Hepworth model notes by the question each answers best. Then explain one link to another heading.

items.label: Hepworth was born in Wakefield.
items.feedback: This is a public life fact. Check the 1903 section of the Estate biography.

items.label: She studied sculpture at the Royal College of Art.
items.feedback: This is a step in her training. Check the 1921–24 section. Training can also shape practice.

items.label: She learnt marble carving from Giovanni Ardini.
items.feedback: This tells us about a making skill. Check the 1925 section. It also links to her training.

items.label: Assembly of Sea Forms is a white marble sculpture.
items.feedback: This names a real work and its material. Check the sculpture’s own caption.

data.discussion: Choose one note. Tell a partner which source would let them check it. A note can link to two headings; explain that link instead of counting one thin fact four times.
data.staffNote: The key shows the best fit for these model questions. Accept a reasoned second connection, especially training and practice. Do not mark a supported connection as wrong just because it crosses a heading.

stages.data-ta2: Use the activity model key in Teacher tools. Discuss a justified different connection; this practice is not an award grade or proof of completed evidence.

stages.title: I Do 2 · connect
stages.data-ta1: Model changing a causal assertion into a research question. Avoid speculative links from life events to mental health, beliefs or intentions.

blocks.text: Here is a common trap. A source names a place where an artist lived. I write: That place made all their art look calm. The place is a fact. My claim about all their art is a leap.

blocks.title: A source and a leap

boxes.head: SUPPORTED
boxes.line1: a public fact in the source

boxes.head: NEEDS A CHECK
boxes.line1: a cause the source does not give

blocks.caption: Do not turn a nearby fact into proof of a cause.
blocks.alt: Boxes labelled SUPPORTED, NEEDS A CHECK. Do not turn a nearby fact into proof of a cause.

blocks.text: I can ask: Did this place affect their work? That is a fair question. To answer it, I need words from the artist or a sound source that makes the link.
I can also give my own view: This work feels calm to me. I label it as my view and point to a feature. It is not a fact about the artist’s life.
Good research can include an honest gap. It does not need a smooth story at the cost of truth.

stages.title: We Do 2 · lab
stages.data-ta1: Pair pupils with reading support as needed. Use the prepared offline extracts when browsing is unavailable, retaining public source links and publisher details. Do not present a search snippet as the full evidence.

blocks.text: Choose a short passage about your own artist. Work with a partner or an adult. First, read it together. Then cover the words and say what you learnt.
Write a short note in your own words. Uncover the source. Check names, dates and meaning. You may keep an exact name or title; you do not need a new word for it.
Now test the trail. Give the checker your source title, link and pack page. Can they find the passage? If not, add the section name or heading.
A search result alone is a clue. Open the source it points to. Check the publisher and the full passage. If two sources disagree, keep both notes and ask for help checking the difference.

stages.title: Independent · evidence
stages.data-ta1: Check all four areas without writing them for the pupil. Supply accessible sources where a gap appears. Scribe only the pupil’s words and retain their reason; numbers of sentences or sources are support choices, not award quotas.

blocks.text: Build your own account under the four headings. Use the real artist you chose. Keep your reason for that choice at the top, or revise it if your research changed your view.
Explain their practice, career, life and work. Include a named work. Put the source beside each fact: publisher, page title and public link. Add the pack page or source section so it is easy to find.
Use your own short words. You can speak, type or write. A scribe may record exactly what you say. Check the words before they join your evidence.

items: Core: use the four headings and question stems. Ask for reading or scribing support. Give your own account of all four areas, your reason and sources.
Extend: write all four areas as a short account. Keep your reason and a source for each fact.
Challenge: keep all four areas and compare what two checked sources add. Explain one limit or difference. Do not invent a fact to fill a gap.

blocks.text: If a heading is empty, return to its question. Ask for the relevant source page. Add what the source supports, not what you think ought to be true. Keep your art question in view while you search.

stages.title: Exit · check and file
stages.data-ta1: Check file-plus-location and retained C1 reason. Record unresolved research areas accurately for follow-up; never mark unchecked or missing evidence as completed.

blocks.text: Read each heading and point to its note. Can you show how the artist makes, a step in their career, a public life fact and a named work?
Choose a fact and test it against the source. Then read your reason for the choice. Does it still fit what you found? You can change your mind and explain why.

Append this account to your existing Bronze-C file. Give the actual file name plus page or slide. For audio, give the file and timecode. Keep the choice and research together rather than making a new file for each fact.
Leave a clear question beside anything still to check. Tell the adult where that gap is. A draft with a named gap is honest work; it is not yet a claim that the part is complete.

print.intro: Use checked sources to explain your artist’s practice, career, life and work. Keep your reason for choosing them and a source beside each fact.
focusRows: Practice: how they make; career: their path in art
Life: an art-relevant public fact; work: a named piece and what it shows
Why chosen; source title, publisher and public URL for each fact; actual Bronze-C file plus page, slide or timecode
tiers: Core: use the four headings, read-aloud support and a verbatim scribe if needed. Give your own account of all four areas, your reason and sources.
Extend: write all four areas in your own short account, with your reason and sources.
Challenge: keep all four areas and compare what two checked sources add. Explain one limit or difference without inventing a fact.
checks: Practice, career, life and work all have distinct information about the real person chosen.
Each fact matches its source; views and unanswered questions are labelled.
My reason for the choice is present and still fits the work I studied.
Evidence joins the existing Bronze-C file with the exact page, slide or timecode.
